segments.text: Feminism is both a political movement and a body of theory built around two connected claims: that women have historically been, and in most societies continue to be, disadvantaged relative to men in rights, resources, and power; and that this disadvantage is not natural or inevitable but the result of social arrangements that can and should be changed.
Feminism as theory vs. feminism as movement.

As theory, feminism analyses why gender inequality exists and persists — through concepts like patriarchy (a social system in which men hold disproportionate power) and the sexual division of labour. As a movement, feminism organises collective action — campaigns, protests, lobbying, legal challenges — to change laws, institutions, and social attitudes.
Common misconceptions worth addressing directly in an answer:

feminism is not a single unified ideology (there are liberal, radical, Marxist/socialist, psychoanalytic, postmodern, and other feminisms, covered in Topics 12–17, which sometimes disagree sharply with each other); it is not inherently anti-men (most feminist theory targets the system of patriarchy, which it argues constrains men as well, see Topic 9); and it is not a purely Western import, since indigenous women’s movements with locally rooted demands exist across Africa, South Asia, and the Muslim world, including Pakistan’s own Women’s Action Forum tradition (Topic 23).
Core shared commitment across all feminist schools:

despite their theoretical disagreements, all feminisms share the basic commitment described above — that gender inequality is real, socially produced, and changeable — which is why they can be treated as a family of related theories rather than as entirely separate fields.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Feminism combines theory (why inequality exists) and movement (organised action to change it).
It is not one ideology but a family of related schools of thought sharing a common core commitment.
It is not confined to the West; locally rooted feminist movements exist across the Muslim world and South Asia.

segments.text: Liberal feminism is historically the earliest and most mainstream strand, rooted in Enlightenment liberal political philosophy — the idea that all individuals possess equal reason and therefore equal rights. Its central claim is that women’s inequality results from unfair exclusion from existing legal, educational, and economic institutions, not from a need to overturn those institutions altogether.
Historical roots and key arguments.

Mary Wollstonecraft’s A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued that women appeared less rational than men only because they were denied the same education, not because of any natural inferiority — if given equal education, women would demonstrate equal reasoning capacity. Later liberal feminists such as John Stuart Mill (The Subjection of Women, 1869) extended this to argue for equal legal and political rights, including suffrage.
What liberal feminism campaigns for, concretely:

equal legal rights (the vote, property ownership, the right to sign contracts), equal access to education, equal employment opportunity and equal pay for equal work, and the removal of formal legal barriers that treat women differently from men (for example, laws historically requiring a husband’s permission for a wife to work or travel).
Strengths:

liberal feminism achieved many of the most visible, concrete legal victories of the feminist movement historically — suffrage, anti-discrimination employment law, and equal-education laws — because its demands (equal treatment under existing law) were relatively achievable within existing political systems.
Criticism.

Radical and Marxist feminists (Topics 13–14) argue that liberal feminism is too limited: achieving formal legal equality does not automatically produce real social equality, because deep structural factors — the unequal distribution of unpaid domestic labour, cultural attitudes, and economic dependency — continue to disadvantage women even after laws are formally equal. Liberal feminism’s critics describe this as mistaking equality on paper for equality in practice.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Liberal feminism seeks equal rights and access within existing institutions, rooted in Enlightenment ideas of equal individual reason.
Wollstonecraft and Mill are its foundational theorists; suffrage and anti-discrimination law are its landmark achievements.
Main criticism: formal legal equality does not remove deeper structural and cultural disadvantages.

segments.text: Radical feminism argues that women’s oppression is the most fundamental and universal form of social inequality, predating and underlying other inequalities like class or race, and that it is rooted directly in the structure of patriarchy itself — men’s systematic control over women’s bodies, sexuality, and labour — rather than merely in unequal laws.
Core claim.

Because the problem is patriarchy as a total social system, radical feminists argue that reform within existing institutions (the liberal feminist approach) cannot be sufficient; the system itself, including its most intimate structures such as the family and heterosexual relationships, needs fundamental transformation.
Key concepts and arguments:

items.text: “The personal is political”

— a foundational radical feminist slogan holding that experiences typically dismissed as private (domestic violence, housework division, sexual relationships) are in fact political, structured by power, and legitimate targets of political analysis and action, not merely private matters.
Control over women’s bodies and sexuality
— radical feminists place particular emphasis on reproductive rights, sexual violence, and pornography as central sites where patriarchal control over women’s bodies is exercised and reproduced.
Patriarchy as a system, not just an attitude

— radical feminists analyse patriarchy as embedded in institutions (family, religion, law, media) that work together to maintain male dominance, rather than as simply a collection of individual sexist attitudes that education alone could fix.

segments.text: Criticism.

Critics argue that treating patriarchy as a single universal system risks flattening major differences in how women experience oppression across different classes, races, and cultures (an objection developed further by intersectional and postcolonial feminists). Some also argue that radical feminism’s focus on heterosexual relationships as inherently structured by domination is too totalising and does not capture the diversity of actual relationships.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Radical feminism sees patriarchy as the foundational, universal structure of inequality, requiring transformation rather than reform.
“The personal is political” reframes private life (housework, sexuality, domestic violence) as a matter of political power.
Criticised for treating patriarchy as a single universal system that may overlook differences of class, race, and culture.

segments.text: Marxist feminism applies Karl Marx’s framework of class and economic exploitation to explain women’s oppression, arguing that it is rooted primarily in the capitalist economic system rather than in patriarchy as an independent structure.
Core argument.

Under capitalism, women perform vast amounts of unpaid domestic labour (childcare, cooking, cleaning) that is essential to reproducing the workforce — feeding and raising the next generation of workers, and allowing male workers to be available for waged labour — but this labour is not recognised or paid, because capitalism benefits from treating it as a “natural” female duty rather than as economically valuable work. Women who do enter the paid workforce are further exploited as a “reserve army of labour” — a pool that can be paid less, hired when convenient, and dismissed first during downturns.
Socialist feminism

is a later refinement that combines the Marxist economic analysis with the radical feminist recognition (Topic 13) that patriarchy is a distinct structure of its own, not simply a by-product of capitalism. Socialist feminists argue that capitalism and patriarchy interact and reinforce each other (sometimes called the “dual systems” theory), so that ending capitalist exploitation alone, without also dismantling patriarchal control, would not automatically end women’s oppression, and vice versa.
Why this distinction matters for policy analysis:

Marxist/socialist feminist theory is the direct theoretical basis for policy demands such as wages for housework, universal public childcare, and paid maternity/parental leave — because these demands treat domestic and reproductive labour as real economic work deserving recognition and compensation, rather than as an unpaid private duty.
Criticism.

Critics note that Marxist feminism, by explaining gender oppression mainly through class and capitalism, can struggle to explain gender inequality in non-capitalist and pre-capitalist societies, which suggests patriarchy has causes independent of capitalism — the very point socialist feminism was developed to address.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Marxist feminism explains women’s oppression through capitalism’s reliance on unpaid domestic labour and women’s use as a flexible “reserve army of labour.”
Socialist feminism refines this with “dual systems” theory: capitalism and patriarchy are distinct but mutually reinforcing structures.
This theory underpins concrete policy demands like paid parental leave and public childcare.

segments.text: Psychoanalytical feminism uses and critically revises Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytic theory to explain how gender identity and gender inequality are formed at the level of early childhood psychological development, rather than only through external social institutions.
Freud’s original theory and the feminist response.

Freud argued that gender identity develops in early childhood partly through children’s recognition of anatomical sex difference, famously through his controversial concept of “penis envy” in girls. Feminist theorists rejected this specific claim as biologically deterministic and demeaning to women, but retained Freud’s broader insight that gender identity is not simply learned consciously through role models — it is formed at a deep, partly unconscious psychological level in early childhood, which is why gender identity feels so stable and “natural” to individuals even though it is, in fact, produced.
Nancy Chodorow’s reworking.

A key feminist revision, from sociologist Nancy Chodorow (The Reproduction of Mothering, 1978), argues that because mothers (not fathers) are typically the primary early caregivers in most societies, girls develop their gender identity in continuous closeness with their mother (leading, Chodorow argues, to relational, empathetic personality traits), while boys must psychologically separate from the mother to form a distinct masculine identity (leading to a personality more oriented toward independence and emotional distance). Crucially, Chodorow argues this pattern is not biologically fixed — it results directly from the social arrangement of assigning mothers as primary caregivers, and would change if caregiving were shared more equally between parents.
Why this matters analytically.

This theory offers a psychological mechanism for why gendered personality traits and the sexual division of labour reproduce themselves generation after generation even without any explicit teaching — children absorb gendered patterns through the emotional structure of early family life itself.
Criticism.

Critics note the theory is difficult to test empirically, relies heavily on culturally specific (largely Western, nuclear-family) assumptions about caregiving arrangements, and may not generalise well to societies with extended-family or communal childcare structures, such as many South Asian household arrangements.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Psychoanalytical feminism examines how gender identity forms unconsciously in early childhood, revising rather than accepting Freud’s original claims.
Chodorow’s theory ties gendered personality differences directly to the social fact that mothers are usually primary caregivers, not to biology.
Its central policy implication: shared parenting could, over generations, reduce gendered psychological patterns.

segments.text: “Men’s feminism,” more precisely referred to in the literature as pro-feminist men’s studies or the study of men and masculinities within a feminist framework, examines how men can engage with, benefit from, and also be harmed by patriarchy, and asks what role men can and should play in feminist politics.
Two distinct strands worth separating in an answer:

items.text: Pro-feminist men’s movements

support feminist goals and argue that men benefit from patriarchy as a group (through greater average access to political power, wages, and social authority) even though individual men also bear costs from rigid masculine norms (Topic 9) — costs such as restricted emotional expression, pressure toward risk-taking, and social stigma for stepping outside prescribed gender roles (for example, men who do full-time caregiving). Pro-feminist men’s advocates argue men have a responsibility to challenge patriarchy precisely because they hold more institutional power to change it.
Men’s rights movements

, by contrast, argue that men face serious, under-recognised disadvantages of their own (in areas like family courts and child custody decisions, workplace safety and occupational fatality rates, or lack of support services for male victims of domestic violence) and are often more openly critical of, or opposed to, mainstream feminist analysis, sometimes framing gender relations as now disadvantaging men more than women in specific domains.

segments.text: Why examiners include this topic.

It tests whether a student can move beyond a simple “men versus women” framing and engage with the more sophisticated relational model of gender (Topic 9) — recognising that a critique of patriarchy as a system is compatible with acknowledging real costs that the same system imposes on men, without treating men’s disadvantages and women’s disadvantages as equivalent in scale or origin.
Balanced conclusion for an exam answer:

the mainstream Gender Studies position is that men’s engagement with feminism is valuable and necessary because patriarchy is a system that shapes both genders, but that specific “men’s rights” claims should be evaluated on their own evidentiary merits case by case, rather than treated as an equal and opposite counter-movement to feminism.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Pro-feminist men’s studies analyses how men both benefit from and are constrained by patriarchy, and calls for men’s active participation in reform.
Men’s rights movements raise specific, separately-evaluated claims about disadvantages men face (custody law, occupational risk) and are often more critical of mainstream feminism.
The relational model of gender (Topic 9) is the key theoretical tool for handling this topic without collapsing into an either/or framing.

segments.text: Postmodern feminism applies postmodern philosophy’s general suspicion of grand, universal explanatory theories to feminism itself, questioning whether concepts like “woman,” “patriarchy,” or “women’s experience” can be treated as single, universal categories at all.
Core argument.

Earlier feminist theories (liberal, radical, Marxist) each proposed a single overarching explanation for women’s oppression, and largely assumed a shared category of “woman” whose interests could be represented collectively. Postmodern feminists, drawing on thinkers such as Michel Foucault (on how power operates through discourse and knowledge, not only through laws and economics) and Judith Butler (Topic 7), argue that this assumption erases real differences among women — of race, class, sexuality, culture, and nationality — and imposes a falsely unified “woman’s experience” that in practice often reflected the specific experience of white, middle-class, Western women.
Key contributions:

items.text: It emphasises that power operates diffusely, through language, everyday practices, and institutions (medicine, education, media) that shape what counts as “normal” gender behaviour, not only through overt legal discrimination.

It rejects the search for one grand theory of women’s oppression (whether patriarchy, capitalism, or psychoanalysis) in favour of examining how gender is constructed differently in different specific contexts.

It laid groundwork for intersectionality (developed most influentially by Kimberlé Crenshaw), the idea that gender, race, and class combine to produce distinct, non-additive forms of disadvantage — a Black working-class woman’s experience of oppression, for example, cannot be understood simply by adding “racism” and “sexism” together, because the two interact to produce a distinct experience.

segments.text: Criticism.

Some feminist scholars (echoing the criticism of queer theory in Topic 7) argue that postmodern feminism’s emphasis on difference and its scepticism toward unified categories makes collective political mobilisation more difficult, since organised movements have historically needed a shared group identity (“women”) to act politically. Postmodernists respond that political coalitions can be built around shared strategic goals without requiring a fixed, essential shared identity.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Postmodern feminism questions whether “woman” and other core feminist categories can be treated as universal, given differences of race, class, and culture.
It draws on Foucault (diffuse power through discourse) and Butler (performativity) and gave rise to intersectionality (Crenshaw).
Main criticism: emphasising difference over unity may weaken the basis for collective feminist political action.
